titre: Fifty Years to Find the Body That Went With These Arms
accroche: In 1965, paleontologists unearth two arms 2.4 meters long in the Gobi, without the rest of the skeleton. It will take until 2014 to discover the whole beast.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 9, 1965, during a Polish-Mongolian expedition in the Gobi Desert, paleontologist Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska unearths a pair of fossilized arms of absurd size: 2.4 meters long each, ending in claws 20 centimeters long. No other part of the skeleton comes with the find. In 1970, Polish paleontologists Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz formally describe the animal under the name Deinocheirus mirificus, “the terrible and strange hand,” for lack of anything better: these two arms are, for now, all that science knows of it.

## Half a Century of Speculation

For nearly fifty years, Deinocheirus remains one of the greatest mysteries in paleontology. What did the rest of the body look like? A giant predatory theropod, bigger than a Tyrannosaurus rex? A distant relative of the ornithomimosaurs, those ostrich-like dinosaurs? The reconstructions published over the decades all contradict one another, for want of a single additional bone to settle it. Several expeditions return to the Gobi to look for the rest of the skeleton, without success.

## Two Skeletons, and a Stolen Piece That Was Missing

The situation breaks open in 2006, when a team spots a partial skeleton at the Altan Uul IV site, without yet knowing whose it is. In 2009, a second team, led by Yuong-Nam Lee, finds a much more complete skeleton at Bugiin Tsav, with arms that at last match those of 1965. But the skull, hands and feet are missing: looters got there before the scientists and sold these pieces on the fossil black market. The French dealer François Escuillié tracks the skull down in a private European collection in 2011, buys it and hands it over to the Belgian paleontologist Pascal Godefroit. The whole is returned to Mongolia on May 1, 2014, a few months before the publication that will finally lift the mystery.

## A Camel With a Backpack and a Duck's Bill

In October 2014, in the journal Nature, Yuong-Nam Lee's team publishes the full description of the animal: 11 meters long, about 6.3 tons, a wide, toothless bill like a duck's, a hump formed by long vertebral spines along the back, and more than 1,400 gastroliths (stones swallowed to grind food) mixed with fish scales in the abdominal cavity. Nothing like a super-predator: it is a giant omnivore, which grazes, fishes and hauls its hump around the wet plains of the Cretaceous in Mongolia, closer to a jury-rigged camel than to the monster that fifty years of speculation had imagined. The solution to the mystery did not lie in a new line of reasoning, but in the two skeletons that had been missing from the start, and in the patience it took to bring them back, piece by piece, out of the earth and then out of the black market.

repere.texte: The two arms found in 1965 are 2.4 meters long each. It would take two more complete skeletons, found in 2006 and 2009, then the return of a stolen skull on May 1, 2014, to publish the full description of the animal in October 2014, forty-nine years later.

carte.punch: They had the monster's arms since 1965. They were only missing the monster.
carte.idee: In 1965, paleontologists unearth two arms 2.4 meters long in the Gobi Desert, and nothing else. It will take two skeletons found in 2006 and 2009 to discover that these terrifying arms belonged to a giant omnivore, grazing and fishing, with a hump on its back.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Detailed overview of the excavation history, the looting of the skull and its return, and the final classification among the ornithomimosaurs.

quiz.question: For fifty years, why did Deinocheirus remain a mystery to paleontologists?
choix: Because its fossils were too fragile to handle
Because only its two arms had been found, with nothing of the rest of the body
Because Mongolia forbade access to the site where it was discovered
Because scientists thought it was a hoax
quiz.explication: The 1965 discovery included only the two arms and the shoulder: no skull, no legs, no spine from which to guess the rest. It was neither fragile fossils nor restricted access that held science back for half a century, but the sheer absence of the missing pieces, found only in 2006 and 2009.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year, and by whom, was Deinocheirus mirificus officially described and named, on the sole basis of the arms found in 1965?
choix: In 1970, by Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz
In 1980, by an anonymous American team
In 2006, by the team that finds the first partial skeleton
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For want of anything else, the Polish paleontologists Halszka Osmólska and Ewa Roniewicz described the animal as early as 1970 under the name Deinocheirus mirificus, from only the arms discovered five years earlier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was the skeleton found in 2009 at Bugiin Tsav not enough, on its own, to solve the mystery?
choix: It actually belonged to a different species from the arms of 1965
The skull, hands and feet were missing, stolen by looters before the scientists arrived
Paleontologists could not fully extract it from the ground before the end of the mission
It was too damaged by erosion to be identified with certainty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Looters got there before the scientists and sold the skull, hands and feet on the fossil black market; it would take until 2011 and 2014 for these pieces to come back, through a dealer and a return to Mongolia.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the full description of Deinocheirus, published in Nature in 2014, reveal about its way of life?
choix: It was a super-predator bigger than a Tyrannosaurus rex
It was an exclusive scavenger, unable to hunt live prey
It was an aquatic animal that never left the rivers
It was a giant omnivore, with a toothless bill, that grazed and fished in wet plains
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2014 description reveals a wide, toothless bill, a dorsal hump, and more than 1,400 gastroliths mixed with fish scales in its abdomen: a giant omnivore, not the super-predator that had long been imagined.
